catalog_quote: p.50: "All four languages are spoken in Benin, but they belong to two different language families: Gur (Yom) and Kwa (Aja, Anii, Foodo). ... All four languages discussed are tone languages, in which intonation is not a primary means for focus realization. The word order is SVO." — p.50 fn.1: "The tone marking follows the following conventions throughout all languages: Every tone is marked (unless otherwise stated) as either high (´), low (`), mid (ˉ), falling (̂) or rising (̌)." — p.52 fn.2: "In most of the Yom example sentences, the tones remain unmarked as their actual value is not clear at the moment." — p.95: "As all sample languages were tone languages (with differing tonal systems), tone already has a heavy functional load and should therefore be excluded from focus marking. Our research so far has shown that variation in F0 and duration can be observed, but they seem only to support syntactic structures" — Fiedler 2006 p.113 fn.4: "The tone marking is as follows: high tone (´), and low tone (`). The downstep following some high tones is marked by (ꜜ)."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (PDFs plus the compiler extracted text dumps). (1) Fiedler 2011 (ISIS 16), p.50 ( lines 44-53): "All four languages are spoken in Benin, but they belong to two different language families: Gur (Yom) and Kwa (Aja, Anii, Foodo).. All four languages discussed are tone languages 1, in which intonation is not a primary means for focus realization. The word order is SVO." -- verbatim as quoted (the only omission is the superscript footnote number 1, whose footnote gives the tone-marking conventions high/low/mid/falling/rising for all four languages). p.52 fn.2 (lines 134-135): "In most of the Yom example sentences, the tones remain unmarked as their actual value is not clear at the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yom is treated as a tone language with two level tones (high, low) plus downstep after some highs; tone carries lexical and grammatical (verb-form/focus) load. Neither open source says anything about word stress or accent placement; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Fiedler 2011 notes the actual tone values of many Yom forms were still unclear to her.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the tonal typology of the language as background to information-structure work (author's own 2005 Djougou fieldwork plus Beacham 1969/1991); not a phonological description. The dedicated phonology (Beacham 1968) was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Yom proper as spoken in Djougou (Donga, Benin), i.e. yomm1242 / ISO pil; Fiedler's consultants were Djougou speakers. The closely related Taneka variety taŋgələm and the sister language Nawdm (nawd1238, Togo) are not covered by these statements.
